Attainment and Attendance in Worthing

What the national model behind How to Pull the Right Lever says about the district’s secondary schools, within West Sussex and alongside Brighton and Hove. Draft for discussion.

Author
Affiliation

Adam Dennett

Bartlett Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, University College London

Published

October 31, 2026

WarningDraft for discussion

One of the district documents for Sussex. It sits beneath the West Sussex document, and the district summary compares all of the districts. Every figure comes from published Department for Education data and the national models of How to Pull the Right Lever. Nothing uses pupil-level records. The commentary is written to a common pattern from the figures; read it as a starting point for discussion.

Summary

Worthing’s results are among the strongest of England’s districts, on an intake less disadvantaged than England’s. Its 6 state secondary schools are in Worthing.

  • Overall results: 49.0 in Attainment 8 in 2024/25, 66th of 264 districts in England.
  • Disadvantage: 17.6% of pupils are disadvantaged, against 28.3% nationally.
  • Disadvantaged pupils average 35.8, below the national 37.8 (146th of 264).
  • The gap between disadvantaged pupils and the rest is 15.9 points, the 33rd widest of 264.

The other findings:

  • For all pupils, Worthing is 2.9 points above England. The largest pieces in the national model are the level of disadvantage (+0.8) and West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-0.7). The district’s schools add 2.4 points beyond what the model expects.
  • For disadvantaged pupils it is 0.0 points below England. The largest pieces are West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-1.5) and being in the South East (-1.3), and the schools add 2.5 points beyond what the model expects.
  • A district effect on the published model disappears once each school’s own record is counted. On the published model Worthing differs from the rest of West Sussex for non-disadvantaged pupils (+3.2%), but that difference belongs to particular schools, not to the place.
  • 5 of the 6 schools are above expectation over 2021/22 to 2024/25. The strongest is St Oscar Romero Catholic School (+6.4); the weakest Bohunt School Worthing (-1.5).
  • Absence was 8.1% in autumn and spring 2025/26 (8.1% a year earlier), against 8.0% for England and 8.1% for West Sussex. Over 2021/22 to 2024/25 its schools ran 0.6 points below what their intakes predict.
  • Reduced timetables run at 2.5 times the national rate, and suspensions at 0.9 times (18.4 per 100 pupils, against 21.2).
  • Disadvantaged groups are small, 23 to 62 pupils a year per school. Every school-level figure for them moves from year to year and should be read over several years.

1 About this analysis

Worthing is a district of West Sussex, not a local authority, and that shapes what can be said:

  • The national models place schools in local authorities. The “local authority effect” in this document is West Sussex’s, shared with every school in the county.
  • What is particular to Worthing shows up in its schools’ own residuals, and in the district test of Section 6.
  • Absence and exclusions are summed over the district’s 6 schools, followed through any change of URN.

The methods are described in full in the East Sussex document.

Across the years the model covers, the gap was 12.6 points in 2021/22 and 15.9 in 2024/25. Worthing’s non-disadvantaged pupils were above England’s average in 4 of 4 years, and its disadvantaged pupils in 2.

4 What explains attainment in Worthing

The decomposition for Worthing, in Attainment 8 points. ‘Place’ is West Sussex’s effect plus the South East’s; ‘unexplained’ is what the district’s own schools add beyond everything the model accounts for.
Factor All pupils Disadvantaged Non-disadvantaged

For all pupils, Worthing is 2.9 points above England. The pieces of at least a quarter of a point:

  • the level of disadvantage (+0.75);
  • West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-0.74);
  • absence (+0.68);
  • being in the South East (-0.46);
  • prior attainment (-0.37);
  • Ofsted ratings (+0.28);
  • and the district’s schools themselves (+2.44), beyond what the model expects.

For disadvantaged pupils, Worthing is 0.0 points below England. The pieces of at least a quarter of a point:

  • West Sussex’s county-wide effect (-1.47);
  • being in the South East (-1.32);
  • absence (+0.83);
  • admissions (-0.30);
  • the level of disadvantage (-0.27);
  • Ofsted ratings (+0.26);
  • and the district’s schools themselves (+2.47), beyond what the model expects.

The level of disadvantage counting against disadvantaged pupils is the Lever report’s most contested finding showing up locally. Across England, disadvantaged pupils do slightly better in schools with more disadvantaged pupils, once everything else is accounted for. The likely reason is that such schools organise around them, and spend pupil premium on provision that a handful of pupils cannot sustain. In Worthing, with 23 to 62 disadvantaged pupils in a year group, that is harder to do.

5 The disadvantaged gap, school by school

No Worthing school is above expectation for its non-disadvantaged pupils while more than a point below it for its disadvantaged ones. Davison Church of England High School for Girls, Worthing, St Andrew’s CofE High School, St Oscar Romero Catholic School, Worthing High School and Durrington High School are above expectation for both groups. The table below gives each school’s own persistent effect, from the model with a school term, which is the steadier measure.

6 Is there a Worthing effect?

The district test of the East Sussex document adds a district level to the national model, with and without each school’s own record.

On the published model, Worthing differs from the rest of West Sussex for non-disadvantaged pupils (+3.2%). With each school’s own record in the model, none of that remains: the difference belongs to particular schools, not to the district as a place.

7 Absence

  • 8.1% absence in autumn and spring 2025/26, against 8.0% for England and 8.1% for West Sussex. A year earlier it was 8.1%.
  • Persistent absence is 20.9%, against 21.6% for England.
  • Against its intake, the district’s schools run 0.58 points below what their pupils’ profiles predict, on average over 2021/22 to 2024/25.
  • No school runs more than a point above its predicted absence.
  • St Oscar Romero Catholic School and Durrington High School run more than a point below their predictions.

Reduced timetables account for 0.72% of sessions, against 0.29% in England, 2.5 times the national rate. Bohunt School Worthing’s rate is the highest in the district.

3 of the 6 schools are above the national average absence in 2024/25. Bringing them to it would add up to 2.3 points for all pupils, as an indication of scale.

Suspensions were 18.4 per 100 pupils in 2024/25, against 21.2 for England and 16.2 for West Sussex.

9 Questions for discussion

  1. Disadvantaged pupils. They average 35.8 in Worthing against 37.8 in England, and the district’s schools add 2.5 points for them beyond what the model expects. What do St Oscar Romero Catholic School and Worthing High School, above expectation for these pupils, do that the district’s other schools could share?
  2. Attendance is not the district’s main lever. Absence adds 0.7 points against England.
  3. Schools, not the place. The district’s apparent effect belongs to particular schools; the question is what is happening in them.
  4. Practice. In Worthing, reduced timetables run at 2.5 times the national rate. These are choices made within schools, and neighbouring districts make them differently.
  5. The county. West Sussex’s own effect for disadvantaged pupils is -3.8% (131st of 151), distinguishable from zero, and it applies to every school here. The county questions in the West Sussex document apply here as well.

Notes on method

Methods and sources are those of the East Sussex document. District membership comes from each school’s postcode (ONS postcode directory, via postcodes.io). Absence and exclusions for the district are summed over its schools, including any predecessor or successor URNs. This document is generated from templates/district_report.qmd by R/20_district_reports.R, from data built by R/17_area_analysis.R, R/18_district_effects.R and R/19_trust_effects.R. Its format is described in AREA_REPORTS.md.
